title: Brocéliande to Joyous Gard: the Best Knight and the Grail He Could Not See
years: c. 502-543 (traditional Arthurian chronology; Camlann fixed, with this atlas, at 537)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Beneath the Lake: the Fostering at Comper

stops.name: Trèbe in Benoic, the birth of Lancelot
stops.campa: In the small kingdom of Benoic, on the border of Gaul and Little Britain, Queen Elaine bears a son to King Ban shortly after Pentecost, in the last free days of a war already lost. The Vulgate names the castle Trèbe; later tradition sets Benoic in the Berry, near Bourges. The child is baptized Galahad for his grandfather, though almost no one in the story will ever call him that again. Claudas of the Land Laid Waste presses the borders daily, and the nurses already speak in whispers of a truce that cannot hold.
suggested_refs: Illuminated Vulgate manuscripts naming Lancelot 'Galahad' at his christening, e.g. BnF Français 122
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the birth of Lancelot, called Galahad)
Nightbringer.se, 'Ban of Benwick'
Wikipedia, 'King Ban'

stops.name: Trèbe, the fall of the last stronghold
stops.campa: Claudas' men, let in by a bribed seneschal, take Trèbe by treachery and put it to the torch while King Ban and his household flee by night. From a hilltop above the road Ban turns to look back at the one tower still his, and watches the flame take it whole. He has no kingdom left to return to. His heart breaks in his chest at the sight, and he falls from his horse dead in the road, a king undone in an afternoon by fire and a servant's greed.
suggested_refs: The motif of the burning tower watched from a hilltop, illustrated in later Lancelot-cycle manuscripts
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the fall of Trebe, the death of King Ban)
Grokipedia, 'King Ban'

stops.name: Comper, Elaine's grief and the taking of the child
stops.campa: Elaine flees on with the infant to the edge of a still lake in the forest of Brocéliande, and sets him down on the bank while she runs the last steps to her dying husband. The Lady of the Lake, who has watched the little company since they crossed into her wood, lifts the child from the grass and carries him down through the water into her hidden palace. Elaine turns back to an empty bank. She takes the veil with her widowed sister Evaine, and the romance calls her ever after the Queen of Great Sorrows.
suggested_refs: The lake and grounds of the Château de Comper, held by tradition as the site of Viviane's hidden palace
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the death of King Ban, the fostering of Lancelot)
lady-of-the-lake.journey.json (shared pin: Comper, the fostering of Lancelot)

stops.name: Comper, the years beneath the lake and the day of arming
stops.campa: Sixteen years pass under the crystal roof no mortal eye can find: the Lady teaches him his letters, the deeds of the old knights, the whole art of arms, and a code of courtesy she folds into him like a second skin, but nothing of his father's ruined kingdom or his own true name. On the day she judges him ready, she arms him in white, sets him on a white horse, and sends him alone toward Camelot to be made a knight, telling him only to give no man his name until he has earned the right to it.
suggested_refs: Illuminated Vulgate manuscripts showing Lancelot's underwater education by the Dame du Lac
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the education and arming of Lancelot)
Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book VI

segments.name: Camelot: the Making of the Knight

stops.name: Winchester (Camelot), the unnamed knighting
stops.campa: The white knight rides into Camelot, which Malory names outright for Winchester, and asks knighthood of Arthur without ever giving his name. Arthur, charmed by the youth's bearing, grants it at once; it is the queen, by the oldest telling, who girds on his sword. He kneels a stranger and rises Sir Lancelot, though even that name is still half a riddle to the court, since no one yet knows he is Ban's son, the boy the Lake raised, come at last to claim a table with an empty seat waiting nowhere near him yet.
suggested_refs: The Winchester Round Table, Great Hall of Winchester Castle, the artefact Malory took for proof of his identification
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the unnamed knighting)
Britannica, 'Camelot'
Wikipedia, 'Camelot' (Malory's identification with Winchester)

stops.name: Bamburgh, Dolorous Gard conquered and renamed
stops.campa: Early in his knight-errantry Lancelot comes to a grim castle the country calls Dolorous Gard, held by Brandin of the Isles behind two gates with ten knights at each. He fights through all twenty, and in the churchyard lifts a great metal slab no unworthy hand can raise: beneath it his own name and lineage, Lancelot of the Lake, son of King Ban, told him for the first time by a grave. Below, past the copper knights, a copper maiden holds two keys; he opens the pillar, then the coffer, and a whirlwind comes out and the enchantments break. Dolorous Gard becomes Joyous Gard.
stops.quote: Some men say it was Alnwick, and some men say it was Bamborough
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter XII (on the identity of Joyous Gard)
suggested_refs: Bamburgh Castle, Northumberland, the site local and Malorian tradition most often names for Joyous Gard
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the conquest of Dolorous Gard)
Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book VI
Wikipedia, 'Joyous Gard'

stops.name: Sorelois (unlocated), the war of Galehaut and the first kiss
stops.campa: Galehaut, lord of many lands, wars against Arthur and stands on the edge of total victory when he sees Lancelot fighting for the losing side and loves him for it, enough to throw the whole war away and submit to a king he could have broken. In gratitude Lancelot becomes his sworn friend, and it is Galehaut who reads the queen's silence and Lancelot's, and pushes their two faces together before the court. A scribe's rubric in a Paris manuscript of the romance marks the moment outright, unlike any before it: how Lancelot kissed the queen the first time. Dante will later call the book itself their Galeotto.
stops.quote: comment mesire lancelot baisa la royne genievre la premiere fois (how my lord Lancelot kissed Queen Guinevere for the first time)
stops.quote_source: Rubric, Lancelot du Lac, BnF Français 118, f. 219v; cf. Dante, Inferno, Canto V
suggested_refs: The manuscript rubric recording the kiss (BnF Français 118, f. 219v), and Dante's reworking of the scene in Inferno V (Paolo and Francesca)
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the war of Galehaut, the first kiss)
Dante, Inferno, Canto V
Dante's Library, Duke University, 'Paolo and Francesca's Book: Lancelot du Lac'

stops.name: Winchester, the best knight living and the secret vow
stops.campa: Within two years of his knighting the court already calls him simply the best knight living, and old Merlin's word about Balin's sword, given long before over the body of that knight, is remembered and repeated at table: that no man shall ever handle it but the best knight of the world, and that shall be Launcelot or his son. No one at this Pentecost yet knows there will be a son. In private, between the two of them alone, Lancelot and the queen swear an oath the romance keeps almost wholly off the page: to love, and to say nothing.
stops.quote: there shall never man handle this sword but the best knight of the world, and that shall be Sir Launcelot or else Galahad his son
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book II, Chapter XIX (Merlin's word on Balin's sword, after the death of Balin)
suggested_refs: Balin's sword, set by Merlin in a floating marble stone and drawn only by Galahad at the Grail Quest
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book II, Chapter XIX
Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the secret oath)

segments.name: The Sword-Bridge into the Kingdom of Gorre

stops.name: The roads of Logres (unlocated), the abduction of the queen
stops.campa: Meleagant, son of King Bademagu of Gorre, rides into Arthur's own land under a knight's challenge and carries off Queen Guinevere while her escort, Kay among them, lies wounded and outmatched on the road. Gorre, Chrétien says outright, is the kingdom from which no traveler returns: a land that answers to no map of Logres and never did. Lancelot, hearing the news, rides out at once with Gawain, wearing out two horses before his own falls dead beneath him, refusing to rest while the queen is a captive of a country with no road marked home from it.
suggested_refs: Chrétien's own line naming Gorre 'the kingdom whence no foreigner returns'
sources: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, ou le Chevalier de la Charrette (trans. W. W. Comfort, 1914)
Wikipedia, 'Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart'

stops.name: On foot on the road, the knight of the cart
stops.campa: Afoot after his second horse dies beneath him, Lancelot meets a dwarf driving an open cart, the kind kept for thieves and traitors led to the pillory, and the dwarf offers word of the queen to whoever will ride in it. Reason tells him plainly that to mount a criminal's cart is a shame no knight lives down; Love, lodged nearer the heart than reason ever gets, tells him to climb up at once. He hesitates two full steps, climbs in anyway, and those two steps of delay, not the climbing itself, are the thing Guinevere will hold against him afterward as the true failure of nerve.
stops.quote: The knight hesitated only for a couple of steps before getting in. Yet, it was unlucky for him that he shrank from the disgrace, and did not jump in at once; for he will later rue his delay.
stops.quote_source: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, or the Knight of the Cart, vv. 247-398 (trans. W. W. Comfort, 1914)
suggested_refs: The cart itself, the medieval pillory-cart, the poem's own emblem of a knight's willingness to be shamed for love
sources: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, or the Knight of the Cart, in Four Arthurian Romances (trans. W. W. Comfort, 1914; Project Gutenberg 831)
GradeSaver, 'Lancelot: Or, the Knight of the Cart'

stops.name: Bath (Gorre), the sword bridge crossed
stops.campa: Chrétien seats King Bademagu's birthday court in his city of Bade, which Foerster reads as Bath, setting the otherworldly kingdom of Gorre astride real Somerset geography even as the poem insists no living stranger returns from it, an honest fold Chrétien never resolves and this record does not smooth over. Two roads lead in, the Water Bridge and the Sword Bridge, a blade's edge stretched over black water. Lancelot chooses the sword, strips the armour from his hands and feet rather than risk a fall, and creeps across on hands, knees and feet, cut to the bone the whole length, and stands on the far bank bleeding and unbeaten.
stops.quote: the king was holding a joyous court at his city of Bade
stops.quote_source: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, or the Knight of the Cart (trans. W. W. Comfort, 1914), with Foerster's note: Bade = Bath
suggested_refs: The Pont de l'Épée as illustrated in later Lancelot-Grail manuscripts, e.g. BnF Français 119
sources: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, or the Knight of the Cart (trans. W. W. Comfort, 1914), text at vv. 6221-6458 and Comfort's footnote 426
Comfort's footnote 414, on the confused topography of the kingdom of Gorre

stops.name: Bath (Gorre), the secret night and the accusation
stops.campa: King Bademagu stops the first duel between Lancelot and his son before it becomes a killing, and lodges the rescued queen and her rescuer under his own roof. That night Lancelot comes secretly to her window, bends the iron bars with his bare bleeding hands, and the wounds from the sword bridge open again and bloody the sheets. In the morning Meleagant, finding blood on the queen's bed and on the bed of her wounded escort Kay, accuses her before the whole court of having lain with the wounded knight; only Lancelot, silent about the true cause, will fight to clear her name.
suggested_refs: The blood-on-the-sheets accusation scene, among the most frequently illustrated moments in Lancelot-Grail manuscripts
sources: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, le Chevalier de la Charrette (trans. W. W. Comfort, 1914)

stops.name: Winchester, the beheading of Meleagant
stops.campa: Godefroi de Leigni, who finishes what Chrétien left unwritten, brings Meleagant to Arthur's own court a year later to press his accusation again and force the duel neither king could put off forever. Lancelot cuts through him without the mercy he shows other men: the right arm falls at one clean stroke, the nose-guard is smashed back through three teeth, the helmet is unlaced and the head comes off. Not a soul present feels any pity. The court that watched a stranger ride off behind a dwarf's cart watches him walk back in as the best knight living.
suggested_refs: The final duel at Arthur's court, the poem's own resolution of the year-long truce sworn at Bademagu's court
sources: Chrétien de Troyes / Godefroi de Leigni, Lancelot, le Chevalier de la Charrette, conclusion
Wikipedia, 'Maleagant'

segments.name: Corbenic: the Deception and the Madness

stops.name: Corbenic (unlocated), the deception of Brisen
stops.campa: Corbenic, castle of the wounded Fisher King Pelles and keeper of the Sangreal itself, has no fixed place on any map the romances agree on; this record marks it, honestly, in the borderlands its illustrators and modern gazetteers most often guess at, not a claimed real site. Pelles' daughter Elaine loves Lancelot past reason and cannot have him, since his whole heart is sworn elsewhere; her handmaid Brisen, skilled in enchantment, brews a wine that makes him believe he lies with Guinevere in a chamber lit only by candles. He does not learn the truth until morning, and by morning Galahad is already begun.
suggested_refs: Corbenic as painted in nineteenth-century Pre-Raphaelite illustration of the Grail cycle
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Queste del Saint Graal / Prose Lancelot (Elaine, Brisen, the conception of Galahad)
Wikipedia, 'Elaine of Corbenic'
P. A. Karr, The Arthurian Companion (on the unlocated geography of Corbenic)

stops.name: Winchester, Guinevere's discovery and the banishment
stops.campa: Word of the deception reaches Camelot, as such things always do, and Guinevere's fury when she learns of it is not jealousy of a rival but the particular rage of a woman who trusted a story could stay simple. She banishes Lancelot from her sight and from court in one sentence, without appeal, and gives no man leave to soften it. He has weathered swords, enchantments, and a year's captivity for her sake, but this single sentence undoes him more completely than any of it; he leaves the hall already half out of his own mind.
suggested_refs: The banishment scene, the hinge between Lancelot's public triumphs and his private unraveling
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (Guinevere's discovery and banishment)
Wikipedia, 'Elaine of Corbenic'

stops.name: The wild country (unlocated), two years mad
stops.campa: Grief and shame close over him at once: he leaps from an open window rather than be looked at, and something in him breaks that no surgeon can set. For two years he wanders the wild country naked or half-clothed, sleeping rough, fighting shepherds for scraps, known to no one and answering to no name at all, not even a false one; that will come later. The court that praised him as the best living knight has no idea where he is; the man who crossed a bridge of swords for the queen now cannot be trusted with a blade at all.
suggested_refs: The madness of Lancelot, a recurring subject in illustrated editions of the Vulgate Cycle
sources: Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the madness of Lancelot)
Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XII

stops.name: Corbenic, the cure and the Joyous Isle
stops.campa: Elaine finds him at last, raving in a garden at Corbenic, and has him carried within reach of the vessel that healed her own father's wound. Brought before the Sangreal itself, still wrapped in its samite, he is cured on the spot, his wits restored as suddenly as they left him. Ashamed to return to Camelot as the man who broke, he takes Elaine's offer instead: a hidden island he names the Joyous Isle, and a false name to wear on it, Le Chevaler Mal Fet, the knight that hath trespassed. Some years of half-borrowed quiet follow, until Ector and Percivale find him.
suggested_refs: The Joyous Isle episode, Lancelot's brief life as Le Chevaler Mal Fet, restored to Camelot by Sir Ector and Sir Percivale
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XII, Chapters IV-VI (the cure by the Sangreal, the Joyous Isle, the false name)
Vulgate Cycle, Prose Lancelot (the cure by the Sangreal, the Joyous Isle)

segments.name: The Grail Quest: the Failure at Corbenic

stops.name: Winchester, the Pentecost vigil and Galahad's arrival
stops.campa: Years pass at court in a peace this record folds rather than pads with invented incident, until a Pentecost eve when a strange old man leads a young knight into the hall and sets him in the one seat at the Round Table always left empty, the Siege Perilous, which has burned every man before who dared it. The boy takes the seat and lives; new letters of gold appear on its edge naming him. Lancelot, watching, already half-guesses what no one has yet said aloud: the boy's face is his own at that age, and the mother's name is Elaine of Corbenic.
suggested_refs: The Siege Perilous, illustrated in countless Grail-cycle manuscripts and in Victorian Grail painting (Rossetti, Burne-Jones)
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XIII, Chapters I-II (the Siege Perilous, Galahad's arrival)
Vulgate Cycle, Queste del Saint Graal

stops.name: A hermitage in the forest (unlocated), the sin named
stops.campa: On the road of the quest a hermit stops Lancelot and reads his whole life back to him without flattery: the greatest knight living, and the least fit of all the fellowship to see the thing he is riding to find. Pride in his own prowess, the hermit says, and the love of a married queen carried for years without repentance, have made him a knight of the world's honor and not of God's. Lancelot does not argue the charge. He confesses fourteen years of hidden sin, weeps, and rides on anyway, because the quest is the one road left that he refuses to turn back from.
stops.quote: never did I battle all only for God's sake, but for to win worship and to cause me to be the better beloved and little or nought I thanked God of it
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XIII, Chapter XX (Lancelot's confession to the hermit)
suggested_refs: The hermit-confessor scenes of the Queste, structurally central to the whole Grail narrative's judgment of the Round Table
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XIII, Chapters XIX-XX (the voice, and the hermit's reproof of Lancelot)
Vulgate Cycle, Queste del Saint Graal

stops.name: Corbenic, struck down before the Grail
stops.campa: The quest brings him back, of all castles in Britain, to Corbenic, where his own son was conceived by a trick he never consented to. A voice warns him at the chamber door not to enter, for what is within is not for sinful eyes; inside he sees, through incense and candlelight, a table of silver and the Sangreal itself, and a mass no living hand should come near without leave. He goes in anyway, to help what he takes for a failing priest, and a breath mixed with fire strikes him down. He lies as a dead man four and twenty days and as many nights.
suggested_refs: The scene of Lancelot struck down before the Grail chamber, contrasted throughout the cycle with Galahad's unveiled sight of the same vessel
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVII, Chapters XIV-XVI
Vulgate Cycle, Queste del Saint Graal (Lancelot's veiled sight of the Grail)

stops.name: Winchester, Agravain's plot and the ambush
stops.campa: Years of guarded peace follow the quest's end, years this record does not pad with invented incident, until Agravain and Mordred, who have hated the secret longer than they have hidden it, tell Arthur outright what the whole court has half-known and never said. Arthur, cornered by his own nephews into acting, rides out hunting and leaves the queen's door watched. Lancelot, warned too late by nothing but habit, comes to her chamber that night anyway and finds a dozen armed knights waiting instead of the queen alone; he kills his way out through men he has fought beside for years.
suggested_refs: The ambush in the queen's chamber, the hinge on which the whole Round Table breaks
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, Chapters I-IV

stops.name: Carlisle, the queen condemned
stops.campa: Arthur, bound by his own law more than by his own wish, condemns Guinevere to be burned outside Carlisle for treason, though the record notes plainly that he does it with a broken heart and no joy in it. His nephews Gareth and Gaheris are made to attend under protest and refuse, out of love for both the queen and Lancelot, to wear armor to the burning, an unarmed mercy that will cost them everything within the hour. The queen is led out in a plain smock to the stake in the field, and the fire is already being laid when the first shout goes up from the watching hill.
suggested_refs: Carlisle Castle and the field of the queen's condemnation, the setting Malory (not Camelot) gives this scene
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, Chapter VII

stops.name: Carlisle, the rescue and the accidental deaths
stops.campa: Lancelot's spies signal from the hill and he comes down on the crowd at full gallop with his kinsmen, cutting the queen loose from the stake in a press of steel and smoke. In the crush he kills men he never meant to touch: Gareth and Gaheris, unarmed as they swore to be, go down under blows meant for armored strangers, and Lancelot does not even know whose bodies he has made until the field clears. It is the single stroke from which the fellowship of the Round Table never recovers, since Gawain will forgive the queen, forgive the war, but never forgive his brothers' deaths.
suggested_refs: The death of Gareth, the event that turns Gawain from Lancelot's staunchest friend into his fixed enemy
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, Chapter VIII

stops.name: Bamburgh (Joyous Gard), the fifteen-week siege
stops.campa: Lancelot carries the queen north to his own castle, and it earns its name again in the hardest way: Joyous Gard becomes the one refuge left to a rescued queen and a knight now called traitor by half the men who once called him friend. Arthur, driven by Gawain's grief past every wish of his own heart, brings the strength of the realm to besiege it. Fifteen weeks the siege holds, Lancelot provisioned and unwilling the whole time to strike a real blow at his own king, sending out only enough force to hold the walls and no more.
suggested_refs: Bamburgh Castle, besieged in the Malorian tradition as Joyous Gard
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, Chapters IX-XVI

stops.name: Bamburgh, the interdict and the exile
stops.campa: Word from Rome breaks the siege before spears do: the Pope, through the Bishop of Rochester, threatens England with interdict unless Arthur takes Guinevere back and accords with Lancelot. Arthur agrees, more from duty to his crown than any wish of his heart, and Lancelot rides the queen from Joyous Gard to Carlisle and gives her back to her husband with his own hands, kneeling to ask a pardon Gawain will not let the king grant. The queen is restored; Lancelot is not. He is given safe passage out of Britain instead, exile dressed as a settlement.
suggested_refs: The Pope's interdict, one of the few moments the Arthurian world touches the real medieval church directly
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, Chapters XVII-XVIII

stops.name: Bayonne (Benwick), Gawain's pursuit
stops.campa: A hundred knights cross with Lancelot to his own inherited lands, which Malory calls Benwick and sets at Bayonne, and he divides the country among Bors, Hector and Lionel as new lords under him. Gawain will not let the matter rest in England and follows with Arthur's whole remaining host to besiege Benwick in turn, a war Lancelot fights half-heartedly, refusing again and again to kill the man he still loves despite everything. Twice Gawain forces a single combat by naming him traitor before both armies, and twice Lancelot beats him nearly to death and stops his own sword rather than finish it.
suggested_refs: The siege of Benwick/Bayonne, the last campaign of the Round Table fought entirely against itself
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, Chapters XIX-XXII

segments.name: Glastonbury: the Last Years and the Ride to Joyous Gard

stops.name: Salisbury Plain, the field of Camlann
stops.campa: News that Mordred has seized the crown and the queen in Arthur's absence calls the king and Gawain home before Benwick falls, and Lancelot, still in France, is left out of the battle that ends everything. On Salisbury Plain, the same ground the Vulgate tradition gives for the Lady of the Lake, Arthur and Mordred kill each other in the day's last exchange, and the fellowship of the Round Table ends in a field of the dead. Lancelot lands days later with his own army, ready at last to fight for his king, and finds a battlefield already gone quiet and a war he came too late to join.
suggested_refs: Salisbury Plain, the site Malory (following the Vulgate) gives for Camlann, distinct from the Cornish Camel/Camelford tradition
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapters I-IV
lady-of-the-lake.journey.json (shared anchor: Camlann, 0537)

stops.name: Amesbury, the last meeting with the queen
stops.campa: He finds Guinevere at last not on a throne but veiled among the nuns of Amesbury, who took her in when the kingdom fell apart around her. She will not let him near her again in this life: she tells the sisters plainly, before he can speak for himself, that through her and Lancelot's love has been wrought all this war and the death of the noblest knights the world has known, her own lord among them. She asks only never to look on his face again, and to be let heal what is left of her soul in what days remain to her.
stops.quote: Through this man and me hath all this war been wrought, and the death of the most noblest knights of the world; for through our love that we have loved together is my most noble lord slain
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter IX
suggested_refs: Amesbury Abbey, since built over, where Guinevere took the veil after Camlann
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter IX

stops.name: Glastonbury, the death and burial of the queen
stops.campa: Lancelot takes the habit at the hermitage of the Archbishop of Canterbury near Glastonbury, where Sir Bedivere is already sheltering, and endures six years of penance there, a twelvemonth of them as an ordained priest singing mass. Then a vision comes three nights running and tells him to haste to Amesbury, for by the time he arrives the queen will be dead. She dies half an hour before he walks in, having prayed two days never to see his face again with worldly eyes. He and his eight fellows carry her the thirty miles back on foot, a hundred torches burning.
suggested_refs: Glastonbury Abbey, the traditional grave of Arthur and Guinevere, exhumed (so the monks claimed) in 1191
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapters X-XI

stops.name: Glastonbury, the death of Lancelot
stops.campa: After her burial he eats and drinks almost nothing, lying night and day grovelling on the tomb of Arthur and Guinevere, until he is dried and dwined away and his own fellows can hardly know him. Within six weeks he takes to his bed, asks his last rites against their protests, and asks that his body be carried to Joyous Gard, because he vowed once to be buried there. That night the hermit-bishop wakes the whole cell laughing: he has seen angels heave Lancelot up, and the gates of heaven opened against him. They find him dead, lying as though he smiled.
stops.quote: here was Sir Launcelot with me with mo angels than ever I saw men in one day. And I saw the angels heave up Sir Launcelot unto heaven, and the gates of heaven opened against him
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter XII (the hermit-bishop's vision on the night of Lancelot's death)
suggested_refs: The death of Lancelot at the hermitage, the bishop's laughter in the night, one of the few unambiguous mercies Malory grants anyone
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter XII

stops.name: Bamburgh (Joyous Gard), borne home for burial
stops.campa: The bishop and nine knights lay him in the same horse bier the queen was carried in and walk him north fifteen days, a hundred torches burning about him, to the one castle that was ever wholly his. At Joyous Gard they set his corpse in the body of the quire fifteen days more, his visage open and naked so that all folk may behold him. Into that service rides Sir Ector, who has searched England, Scotland and Wales seven years for his brother. He is buried there with great devotion, the map complete but for the one country he never entered.
stops.quote: thou were the courteoust knight that ever bare shield. And thou were the truest friend to thy lover that ever bestrad horse. And thou were the truest lover of a sinful man that ever loved woman. And thou were the kindest man that ever struck with sword
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter XIII (Sir Ector's lament over the body of Lancelot at Joyous Gard)
suggested_refs: Sir Ector's lament, among the most quoted passages in all of English prose, still read at the close of Arthurian retellings
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapters XII-XIII
